title: Radio Line-of-Sight Calculator: The 4/3 Earth
description: Calculate radio line of sight between antennas with the Radio Line-of-Sight Calculator — geometric and 4/3-Earth radio horizons compared. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, two 30 m antennas enjoy a radio horizon of about 45.2 km between them — the air's refraction stretches their reach some 6 km past the 39.1 km that pure geometry allows.
quick_answer: The Radio Line-of-Sight Calculator computes how far two antennas can see each other, comparing the pure geometric horizon with the 4/3-Earth radio-horizon model that accounts for atmospheric refraction. Enter both antenna heights and read each model's range — the first number every radio link plan stands on.

A repeater's service edge is its horizon against the users' antenna heights — this page draws that circle honestly, twice (guaranteed and typical).
Beyond-FM-simplex range questions are horizon questions. Two home stations at 10 m talk across about 26 km of radio horizon on flat land — terrain permitting, as always.
Tropospheric ducting can multiply ranges many-fold on special days — the calculator's standard model is the baseline those miracles are measured against.

A 100 m tower against a 10 m rooftop: geometric range 35.7 + 11.3 = 47.0 km; radio range 41.2 + 13.0 = 54.2 km. Refraction hands the planner 7 km — on standard days. Links engineered to need the gift on all days are engineered to fail on some.

Two handhelds at head height (1.8 m): radio horizons of about 5.5 km each, 11 km combined over perfect flatness. Real terrain, trees and buildings take their cut from there — which matches every hiker's experience of '5-mile' radios.

popular_table.note: Antenna height means height above the surrounding terrain along the path — a 30 m mast in a deep valley starts its horizon from the valley's terms, not the sea's.

faq: Does antenna gain extend the horizon?

Gain focuses power — it extends the range at which a usable signal arrives once a path exists, but it does not bend the horizon. Beyond-horizon paths need refraction luck, diffraction loss budgets, or a relay.
What about diffraction over a ridge?
Signals do bend over knife edges at a loss — engineered paths sometimes use it deliberately. This page computes the clean-horizon models; diffraction design is the path engineer's next layer.
HF signals refract off the ionosphere and ignore horizons entirely; VHF and up are the horizon-bound world this page serves. Frequency also fattens the Fresnel zone — the other half of link planning.
Height above sea level or above ground?
Above the terrain the path crosses — the horizon forms against the local surface. A mountain-top site's sea-level elevation is famous precisely because it is also its path advantage.

Under sub-refraction (unusual temperature/humidity gradients) the effective Earth can shrink below even the geometric case — coastal and desert paths know these moods. Conservative designs keep margin for them.
Add their separate horizons — the table's rows are per-antenna contributions, which is why one tall site serves so many small ones.
A 1.5–2 m vehicle whip lives in the handheld row of the table: roughly 11 km of ideal combined range to another vehicle, before terrain edits it.
